newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda trial witness clashes with accused.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda trial witness clashes with accused.

text.p: A 70-year-old female witness to the U.N.'s Rwanda tribunal clashed on Thursday with the mayor of her commune accused of genocide during an hour of acrimonious cross-examination.
The witness objected to questions from accused Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, the former mayor of Rwanda's Taba commune, saying they both knew what crimes he had committed.
"Did you just come to make me lose my mind by asking these questions," she said after Akayesu asked her to restate the detail of her testimony.

Akayesu is accused of genocide and crimes against humanity in mass killings of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus sparked off by the assasination of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana.
Angry Habyarimana supporters took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to his junta.

On Wednesday the elderly Hutu witness known as "N" to protect her identity told the court she was severely beaten by Akayesu, tied up and forced to lie in front of his car while he threatened to drive over her.
Akayesu's beating broke bones in her back and she could no longer work or dress herself, she said.
"When you say a car is driven over somebody what do you mean," Akayesu asked the woman.
"Did you not want to crush me with that car? You told me to lie down on the ground and you were going to drive over me to crush me," the woman replied.

She also said she watched him give a speech during the 1994 genocide inciting Hutus to kill Tutsis and disembowel Hutu women pregnant by Tutsi men. In Rwanda ethnicity is determined by the paternal line.
Two previous witnesses had also testified to the speech, crucial to the prosecution case that genocide was committed in Taba commune.

Akayesu has pleaded not guilty to genocide, which ended only when Tutsi rebels now in power drove the Hutu army into exile in Tanzania, Zaire and Kenya. The defendant, who wants to dismiss his lawyers, asked questions under tribunal rules which allow him to cross-examine witnesses directly.
Akayesu dressed in a dark suit and open-necked shirt looked at ease with court proceedings in contrast to the woman, who was at first bewildered by the formality of the tribunal.
But his cross-examination did not appear designed to undermine testimony that he personally ordered Tutsis killed and tortured and beat Hutus and Tutsis who opposed him.

Presiding Judge Laity Kama of Senegal adjourned the court until the afternoon when the prosecution was to call the fourth of its 31 witnesses. Officials said they expected the witness to be a doctor with aid agency Doctors Without Borders (MSF), the tribunal's first expert witness.
Akayesu is the first suspect tried before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, set up in November 1994 to bring to justice the central figures in the genocide.
Tribunal officials say they hope the start of trials will improve the image of the tribunal, hit by allegations of mismanagement, racism and financial malpractice and riven by internal divisions.
Rwanda also opened its own genocide trials and already two people have been sentenced to death. They face death by firing sqaud if their appeals are turned down.
